text:
PREMISE: The deficit grew because we spend too much on the poor.

STEP 1: CBO: the FY2026 deficit was about $2.0 trillion, up $218 billion from FY2025 (preliminary).
STEP 2: The biggest single jump in spending was net interest on the debt, up $115 billion.
STEP 3: Spending on food and nutrition programs fell $11 billion, mainly from fewer people on SNAP.
STEP 4: Corporate income tax receipts fell $70 billion.

CONCLUSION: The poor got less, and the deficit still grew. Look at interest and corporate taxes, not food aid.

PREMISE: Defense is the biggest driver of the deficit.

STEP 1: Defense spending did rise, by $48 billion, to $916 billion.
STEP 2: Net interest rose more, by $115 billion, to $1.143 trillion.
STEP 3: Social Security rose $86 billion and Medicare $77 billion, mostly from more retirees and higher costs.
STEP 4: Revenue grew $169 billion. Spending grew $386 billion.

CONCLUSION: Many things raised the deficit. The biggest single riser was interest. Name all the causes, and the largest first.

PREMISE: Interest on the debt is a small line item.

STEP 1: CBO: net interest hit $1.143 trillion in FY2026.
STEP 2: That's more than defense at $916 billion.
STEP 3: It's more than Medicaid at $723 billion.
STEP 4: Borrowing to pay for tax cuts at the top adds to that bill every year.

CONCLUSION: Bondholders now get paid more than soldiers or Medicaid patients. That's a priority choice.

PREMISE: Everyone's paying their share of taxes.

STEP 1: CBO: individual income tax receipts rose 7% in FY2026, to $2.844 trillion.
STEP 2: Payroll taxes rose 4%, to $1.815 trillion.
STEP 3: Corporate income taxes fell 16%, to $382 billion.
STEP 4: CBO says the drop came from bigger investment write-offs in the 2025 law.

CONCLUSION: Workers paid more. Corporations paid less. That's a shift, not a coincidence.

PREMISE: Corporate taxes fell because companies made less money.

STEP 1: BEA: corporate profits from current production rose $384 billion in the second quarter of 2026 (annual rate).
STEP 2: CBO: corporate tax receipts fell 16% for FY2026.
STEP 3: CBO says rising corporate income would have raised payments, but new deductions offset it.
STEP 4: Different time frames, same direction: profits up, taxes down.

CONCLUSION: The tax drop came from the law, not from poor companies.

PREMISE: The corporate tax cuts are paying for themselves.

STEP 1: If cuts paid for themselves, receipts would hold steady or rise.
STEP 2: Corporate receipts fell $70 billion, or 16%, in FY2026.
STEP 3: The deficit rose $218 billion the same year.
STEP 4: Profits rose. Tax payments didn't follow.

CONCLUSION: Check the receipts, not the promise. This one didn't pay for itself.

PREMISE: Tariff refunds are just paperwork after a court case.

STEP 1: The Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in February 2026 that IEEPA doesn't let the president impose tariffs.
STEP 2: CBP reported about $100 billion in refunds completed by the end of July 2026.
STEP 3: Refunds go to importers who paid the duties.
STEP 4: Shoppers who paid higher prices have no refund line.

CONCLUSION: Businesses get their money back. Customers who paid the markups don't. Ask where the refund lands.
sources: CBP filing via Tribune India, Aug. 2026

text:
PREMISE: We had to cut SNAP to get the deficit under control.

STEP 1: Federal food and nutrition spending fell about $11 billion in FY2026.
STEP 2: Tariff refunds to importers reached about $100 billion by July.
STEP 3: Corporate tax receipts fell $70 billion.
STEP 4: The deficit still rose $218 billion.

CONCLUSION: The SNAP savings were small next to the money flowing to businesses. The deficit was never the real reason.
sources: CBP filing via Tribune India, Aug. 2026

text:
PREMISE: Prices are under control. Core inflation is only 2.4%.

STEP 1: Core inflation leaves out food and energy. Economists use it to see the trend. That's fair.
STEP 2: Families still buy gas and power. Energy prices rose 16.3% in the year to August.
STEP 3: Gasoline rose 27.4%, the biggest single driver of inflation.
STEP 4: Working families spend a bigger share of income on gas and utilities than the rich.

CONCLUSION: Core shows the trend. Headline shows the bill. Working people pay the headline.

PREMISE: Wages went up 3%. Workers are doing fine.

STEP 1: BLS: average hourly pay rose 3.0% over the year to September, to $37.81.
STEP 2: Consumer prices rose 3.4% over the year to August.
STEP 3: Pay that rises slower than prices is a real pay cut.
STEP 4: Labor's share of business income hit a record low of 52.8% in Q2 2026.

CONCLUSION: A raise below inflation is a cut. Meanwhile owners took a bigger slice.

PREMISE: Gas prices hurt everyone the same.

STEP 1: Gasoline rose 27.4% in the year to August.
STEP 2: A worker commuting 40 miles a day in rural Louisiana burns far more gas than a remote worker in a city.
STEP 3: Low-income households spend a bigger share of income on fuel.
STEP 4: Wages rose 3.0%.

CONCLUSION: The same price hike takes a bigger bite from rural and low-wage workers.

PREMISE: High oil prices are great for Louisiana workers.

STEP 1: Gasoline prices rose 27.4% in a year.
STEP 2: BLS: Louisiana mining and logging jobs, which include oil and gas extraction, fell 2.1% from July 2025 to July 2026 (preliminary).
STEP 3: Higher prices raise producer revenue. They don't automatically add jobs.
STEP 4: Louisiana drivers pay more at the pump either way.

CONCLUSION: Oil profits and oil jobs aren't the same thing. Ask who keeps the windfall.
sources: BLS Louisiana Economy at a Glance, July 2026

text:
PREMISE: Anyone who wants a job can find one.

STEP 1: BLS: 7.1 million people were unemployed in September.
STEP 2: JOLTS: there were about 7.1 million job openings in August.
STEP 3: That's roughly one opening per jobless person, and openings don't always match where people live or their skills.
STEP 4: 1.9 million people have been looking for six months or more.

CONCLUSION: When there's about one job per job seeker, 'just get a job' isn't a plan.

PREMISE: Workers have all the leverage now. They can quit anytime.

STEP 1: JOLTS: the quit rate was 1.9% in August.
STEP 2: People quit when they're confident they'll find something better.
STEP 3: A low quit rate means workers are staying put, often out of caution.
STEP 4: Wage growth slowed to 3.0%, below inflation.

CONCLUSION: Low quits mean low leverage. That's when organizing matters most.

PREMISE: The first jobs number tells you how the economy is doing.

STEP 1: BLS first reported 21,000 jobs added in July. It's now revised to a loss of 10,000.
STEP 2: August was revised down from 162,000 to 133,000.
STEP 3: Together, July and August were 60,000 lower than first reported.
STEP 4: September's 29,000 will be revised too.

CONCLUSION: First numbers are drafts. Watch the revisions before you celebrate or panic.

PREMISE: Black unemployment is a separate issue from the overall job market.

STEP 1: Black unemployment rose to 7.0% in September.
STEP 2: White unemployment was 3.6%. Overall, 4.2%, the highest since 2021.
STEP 3: Black workers are often hit first when hiring slows.
STEP 4: Overall unemployment rose the same month.

CONCLUSION: Black unemployment is the early warning. When it climbs, everyone's job is at risk.

PREMISE: People who lost SNAP must have found jobs.

STEP 1: USDA: SNAP enrollment fell by more than 5.3 million, about 12.8%, from June 2025 to June 2026.
STEP 2: Over roughly the same time, unemployment rose to 4.2%, the highest since 2021.
STEP 3: 1.9 million people were unemployed for six months or more in September.
STEP 4: Need didn't fall. The rolls did.

CONCLUSION: Fewer people on SNAP doesn't mean less hunger. Check the job numbers before you claim success.

PREMISE: Louisiana's SNAP drop shows the state removed noncitizens.

STEP 1: Test the claim against the state's own data.
STEP 2: Louisiana SNAP enrollment fell nearly 21% in a year, about 166,000 fewer people a month.
STEP 3: The Louisiana Department of Health said none of the closures came from failed citizenship checks.
STEP 4: LDH said about 75% of closures since July 2025 were procedural, like missing paperwork.

CONCLUSION: The chain breaks. Most people lost food aid over paperwork, not citizenship. Blame the red tape, not immigrants.

PREMISE: Louisiana SNAP cuts only affect adults who won't work.

STEP 1: Children on Louisiana SNAP fell by 82,064, about 23%, from July 2025 to June 2026.
STEP 2: That was the biggest drop of any group.
STEP 3: Children aren't subject to work requirements.
STEP 4: Most closures were procedural.

CONCLUSION: When paperwork drops a parent, the kids lose food too.

PREMISE: The new SNAP rules don't cost states anything.

STEP 1: Starting October 2026, states pay half of SNAP administrative costs, up from 25%.
STEP 2: Starting October 2027, states with error rates above 6% begin losing some federal benefit funding.
STEP 3: Louisiana's payment error rate is 8.14%.
STEP 4: Analysts warn states may cut rolls to cut errors. LDH says closures and error rates aren't linked.

CONCLUSION: Federal cost shifts create pressure on state budgets. Watch whether that pressure lands on families.

PREMISE: Child poverty hit a record low, so the cuts aren't hurting kids.

STEP 1: Census: the official child poverty rate fell to 13.4% in 2025, a historic low.
STEP 2: That data covers 2025, before most of the SNAP and Medicaid changes hit.
STEP 3: Louisiana child SNAP enrollment fell 23% by June 2026.
STEP 4: The 2026 numbers come out next fall.

CONCLUSION: Check the dates. Last year's good news can't measure this year's cuts.

PREMISE: The uninsured rate held steady, so Medicaid changes didn't matter.

STEP 1: Census: 26.7 million people, 7.9%, were uninsured for all of 2025, about the same as 2024.
STEP 2: Medicaid coverage dipped to 17.1% in 2025.
STEP 3: KFF: Medicaid enrollment fell 5.1 million, about 6%, from June 2025 to June 2026 (preliminary).
STEP 4: Work requirements haven't started yet.

CONCLUSION: The 2025 survey came before the 2026 drop. Expect the uninsured count to rise.

PREMISE: Cutting Medicaid rolls will save money.

STEP 1: KFF: Medicaid enrollment fell about 6% in a year.
STEP 2: CBO: federal Medicaid spending still rose 8% in FY2026, to $723 billion.
STEP 3: CBO says the main reason is rising costs per enrollee.
STEP 4: Fewer people covered didn't mean lower spending. Prices drive the bill.

CONCLUSION: If costs per person drive spending, go after prices, not people.

PREMISE: When people lose Medicaid, the cost disappears.

STEP 1: People who lose coverage still get sick.
STEP 2: They show up at emergency rooms, which must treat them.
STEP 3: Hospitals absorb unpaid care, and rural hospitals are the most fragile.
STEP 4: Medicaid enrollment fell 5.1 million in a year.

CONCLUSION: Uncovered care doesn't vanish. It moves to ERs, hospitals and everyone's premiums.

PREMISE: Louisiana's Medicaid work requirements will barely touch anyone.

STEP 1: State health officials estimated about 21,000 could lose coverage when requirements start in 2027.
STEP 2: They called 100,000 the absolute worst case.
STEP 3: Louisiana's SNAP experience: about 75% of closures were procedural.
STEP 4: Paperwork, not work, is what usually drops people.

CONCLUSION: The state's own estimate is tens of thousands. If SNAP is a preview, paperwork will decide the final count.

PREMISE: People without jobs should just meet the work requirement.

STEP 1: Medicaid work rules require 80 hours a month.
STEP 2: BLS: 4.5 million people work part time because they can't get full-time hours.
STEP 3: 1.9 million have been jobless six months or more.
STEP 4: There's about one job opening per unemployed person.

CONCLUSION: A work requirement in a slowing job market punishes people for the economy.

PREMISE: Lose your job, go on Medicaid. The safety net catches you.

STEP 1: Census: 53.5% of people had employer-based coverage in 2025.
STEP 2: Unemployment rose to 4.2% in September.
STEP 3: Medicaid enrollment fell 5.1 million in a year.
STEP 4: The net is shrinking just as job losses rise.

CONCLUSION: Job insurance and health insurance are tied together. Cut both at once and people fall through.

PREMISE: The rich and the poor are both doing better this year.

STEP 1: Fed: the top 1% held 32.5% of household wealth in Q2 2026, up from 31.1% a year earlier.
STEP 2: The bottom half held 2.3%, down from 2.4%.
STEP 3: Over the same year, SNAP fell by 5.3 million people and Medicaid by 5.1 million.
STEP 4: Wealth went up at the top while aid went down at the bottom.

CONCLUSION: Not everyone is rising. The gap is.
sources: Federal Reserve DFA via FRED, Q2 2026

text:
PREMISE: Record median income proves the economy works for working people.

STEP 1: Census: median household income hit a record $87,460 in 2025, up 2.6%.
STEP 2: Income is what you earn. Wealth is what you own.
STEP 3: The top 1% raised their wealth share to 32.5% by mid-2026.
STEP 4: Real pay is now slipping, with wages up 3.0% and prices up 3.4%.

CONCLUSION: A good income year doesn't close a wealth gap. And 2026 is going the other way.

PREMISE: Profits and paychecks rise and fall together.

STEP 1: BEA: corporate profits rose $384 billion in Q2 2026 (annual rate).
STEP 2: BLS: labor's share of business income hit a record low, 52.8%, the same quarter.
STEP 3: Real hourly compensation fell at a 3.3% annual rate that quarter.
STEP 4: Profits rose while workers' share shrank.

CONCLUSION: The pie grew. Owners took the new slices.

PREMISE: GDP is growing, so jobs will follow.

STEP 1: BEA: real GDP grew at a 2.2% annual rate in Q2 2026.
STEP 2: By September, employers added just 29,000 jobs.
STEP 3: Profits rose sharply in Q2, and labor's share fell.
STEP 4: Growth that goes to profits doesn't automatically hire.

CONCLUSION: Ask who the growth went to before assuming it'll trickle into jobs.

PREMISE: Household debt fell, so families are getting healthier.

STEP 1: NY Fed: total household debt fell $13 billion in Q2 2026, to $18.8 trillion.
STEP 2: That came from mortgages, down $74 billion.
STEP 3: Credit card debt rose $21 billion, to $1.26 trillion. Auto loans rose $28 billion.
STEP 4: With real pay slipping, many families are putting basics on cards.

CONCLUSION: Look inside the total. Card debt rising while pay lags is a warning, not a recovery.
sources: NY Fed Household Debt and Credit, Q2 2026

text:
PREMISE: Social Security is a burden on the budget.

STEP 1: CBO: Social Security cost $1.654 trillion in FY2026.
STEP 2: Census: it moved 28.8 million people out of poverty in 2025, more than any other program.
STEP 3: Workers pay in through payroll taxes, which rose 4% to $1.815 trillion.
STEP 4: Wages above $184,500 pay nothing in.

CONCLUSION: It's the best anti-poverty buy in the budget. If it needs money, lift the cap.

PREMISE: Groceries are getting cheaper, so SNAP cuts are fine.

STEP 1: Food at home prices still rose 2.2% in the year to August.
STEP 2: Prices rising more slowly is not prices falling.
STEP 3: SNAP rolls fell 5.3 million over the year to June.
STEP 4: Louisiana's average benefit is about $189 a month per person.

CONCLUSION: Food still costs more, and fewer people have help paying for it.

PREMISE: Restaurant prices are up, so servers must be making more.

STEP 1: Food away from home rose 3.4% in the year to August.
STEP 2: The federal tipped minimum is still $2.13 an hour, unchanged since 1991.
STEP 3: Higher menu prices go to the owner first.
STEP 4: Servers' base pay hasn't moved in 35 years.

CONCLUSION: Rising prices don't raise a frozen wage. Customers pay more; the floor stays at $2.13.

PREMISE: Rent is under control now.

STEP 1: Concede the good news: rent rose 2.7% in the year to August, a bit below wage growth.
STEP 2: Slower growth still adds to an already high base.
STEP 3: LSUS found 48.4% of Louisiana renters were cost-burdened in 2023.
STEP 4: Energy and gas costs rose much faster, squeezing the same budgets.

CONCLUSION: Cooling rent growth helps. It doesn't undo years of high rents. Say both.

PREMISE: Power bills are a minor expense.

STEP 1: Electricity prices rose 3.8% and utility gas 4.4% in the year to August.
STEP 2: Both outpaced wage growth of 3.0%.
STEP 3: In a Louisiana summer, AC isn't optional.
STEP 4: When bills go unpaid, shutoffs follow.

CONCLUSION: Utility costs rising faster than pay is a health risk on the Gulf. No shutoffs in heat waves.

PREMISE: Louisiana's unemployment is fine, so poverty must be about effort.

STEP 1: BLS: Louisiana's unemployment rate was 4.4% in July 2026 (preliminary), close to the national rate.
STEP 2: Louisiana still has the nation's highest poverty rate, 19.7% (official, 2023–2025).
STEP 3: Joblessness isn't unusually high. Poverty is.
STEP 4: That points to low pay: a $7.25 floor and no state minimum wage law.

CONCLUSION: Jobs without decent pay don't end poverty. The problem is wages, not effort.
sources: BLS Louisiana Economy at a Glance, July 2026

text:
PREMISE: Louisiana's construction boom proves the economy is strong.

STEP 1: Louisiana construction jobs rose 11.4% in a year (July 2026, preliminary).
STEP 2: Information jobs fell 6.3% and mining and logging fell 2.1%.
STEP 3: Much of the construction comes from big industrial and LNG projects.
STEP 4: Building a plant takes far more workers than running it.

CONCLUSION: A construction boom is real, and temporary. Ask what's left when the cranes leave.
sources: BLS Louisiana Economy at a Glance, July 2026

text:
PREMISE: Teens need looser child labor laws so they can work.

STEP 1: BLS: teen unemployment was 14.5% in September.
STEP 2: Teens who want jobs already can't find them.
STEP 3: Looser rules mean longer hours and riskier tasks for kids already working, not more jobs.
STEP 4: Illegal child labor cases were already at record levels.

CONCLUSION: The teen problem is too few jobs, not too many protections.

PREMISE: People are unemployed because they don't want to work.

STEP 1: 4.5 million people work part time but want full-time hours.
STEP 2: 1.9 million have looked for work for six months or more.
STEP 3: Quits are low, a sign people are holding on to jobs.
STEP 4: There's about one opening per unemployed person.

CONCLUSION: The data shows people wanting work, not avoiding it.

PREMISE: Prices are rising faster than the official numbers say.

STEP 1: BEA's PCE price index rose at a 5.0% annual rate in Q2 2026. That's one quarter, annualized.
STEP 2: BLS's CPI rose 3.4% over twelve months to August.
STEP 3: Different measures and time frames give different numbers.
STEP 4: Both show prices beating the 3.0% pay increase.

CONCLUSION: Don't cherry-pick the scariest number. Every measure says the same thing: pay is behind prices.

PREMISE: These numbers prove we're in a recession.

STEP 1: Some warning signs: unemployment at a four-year high, weak hiring, downward revisions, rising Black unemployment.
STEP 2: Other signs: GDP grew at 2.2% in Q2, and openings still roughly match job seekers.
STEP 3: A recession is a broad decline, and it's usually called after the fact.
STEP 4: The honest read is 'slowing, with risks rising.'

CONCLUSION: Don't overclaim. 'Slowing and getting worse for workers' is true and strong enough.

PREMISE: Health care jobs will carry the economy no matter what.

STEP 1: Health care added 17,000 jobs in September, about half its 12-month average of 33,000.
STEP 2: Nursing and residential care lost 9,000 jobs.
STEP 3: Medicaid is a major payer for nursing homes.
STEP 4: Medicaid enrollment fell 5.1 million in a year.

CONCLUSION: Cut the payer and you can expect pressure on the jobs it funds. Watch care jobs closely.

PREMISE: Medicare and Social Security costs are out of control.

STEP 1: CBO: Medicare rose 8% and Social Security 5% in FY2026.
STEP 2: More people are retiring. Prices for care keep rising.
STEP 3: Census: Medicare covered 20.1% of people in 2025, up 0.6 points.
STEP 4: Private coverage for people 65 and older fell 2.8 points.

CONCLUSION: Growing costs reflect more retirees and pricey care. Fix prices and funding, not benefits.

PREMISE: Washington's budget fights don't touch Louisiana.

STEP 1: Federal SNAP cost shifts begin in October 2026. Louisiana's error rate of 8.14% exposes it to penalties from 2027.
STEP 2: Louisiana SNAP rolls fell about 166,000 people a month in a year.
STEP 3: Medicaid work rules start in 2027. The state estimates about 21,000 could lose coverage.
STEP 4: Louisiana has the nation's highest poverty rate.

CONCLUSION: Federal choices land on Louisiana families first and hardest.

PREMISE: The tariffs protected workers. Losing them in court hurt workers.

STEP 1: The Supreme Court ruled in February 2026 that IEEPA doesn't authorize tariffs.
STEP 2: Refunds of about $100 billion went to importers.
STEP 3: Manufacturing added 9,000 jobs in September and 72,000 since December 2025.
STEP 4: Tariffs are one factor in factory jobs among many: demand, rates, investment.

CONCLUSION: Don't credit or blame one policy for a trend with many causes. Look at who got the money: importers.
sources: CBP filing via Tribune India, Aug. 2026

text:
PREMISE: Credit card debt is a personal responsibility issue.

STEP 1: Card balances rose $21 billion in one quarter, to $1.26 trillion.
STEP 2: Gas rose 27.4% and energy 16.3% in a year.
STEP 3: Wages rose 3.0%.
STEP 4: About 4.7% of household debt was delinquent in Q2.

CONCLUSION: When basics outrun pay, families borrow. That's math, not irresponsibility.

PREMISE: Louisiana's 8% SNAP error rate proves the program is riddled with fraud.

STEP 1: Louisiana's payment error rate is 8.14%, above the 6% federal threshold.
STEP 2: A payment error means a benefit was paid wrong. It counts underpayments as well as overpayments.
STEP 3: USDA says error rates measure mistakes by states and households, not fraud.
STEP 4: LDH says Louisiana's rate is the 16th lowest in the country.

CONCLUSION: Errors are a reason to fix the system, not proof of fraud. Don't let a paperwork number become a smear.
sources: USDA FNS payment error rate guidance

text:
PREMISE: Government data is too dry to move people.

STEP 1: CBO: interest beat defense and Medicaid.
STEP 2: BLS: pay is behind prices, and the jobless rate is at a four-year high.
STEP 3: USDA: millions lost food aid. In Louisiana, mostly over paperwork.
STEP 4: The Fed: the top 1% grew its share while the bottom half shrank.

CONCLUSION: Put the numbers side by side and they tell one story: who pays, who gains. Bring receipts.
